entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Thomas Morton (c. 1580s–1647?) was an English lawyer, trader, and satirical writer best known for his New England venture at Merrymount (Mount Wollaston) and for New English Canaan (1637), a book that mocked Puritan severity while praising Native hospitality and commercial liberty. Though sometimes labelled a playwright in loose catalogues, his lasting literary mark is this polemical prose romance of colonial manners.

Morton’s Maypole revels and fur-trade alliances angered Plymouth and Massachusetts authorities, who arrested and banished him more than once. His conflict dramatised early struggles over authority, pleasure, and Indigenous exchange in English America—royalists and Anglicans versus godly magistrates.

Modern scholars read Morton as an anti-Puritan witness: flawed, self-interested, yet invaluable for recovering alternative colonial visions suppressed by winners’ histories.
